stories.headline: Luxury Pajama-Maker Derek Rose Steps Out of the Bedroom, and Onto the Street, With a New Collection
stories.claim: Derek Rose, the 100-year-old British nightwear maker, launches a menswear ready-to-wear collection to mark its anniversary.
stories.summary: British luxury pyjama-maker Derek Rose, founded in 1926, is stepping out of nightwear with a new menswear ready-to-wear collection for its centenary. The range includes Italian merino knits, denim, corduroy, cotton-cashmere trousers and flannel shirts, priced from £210 for cotton-cashmere lounge trousers to £775 for a wool and cashmere ribbed sweater. Chief executive Sacha Rose, whose grandfather founded the business, says the brand is now promoting itself more actively and aims for measured growth. Ready-to-wear and loungewear now make up 70 per cent of the business, with pyjamas at 30 per cent. The UK is its largest market, followed by the US, and it sells through three London stores and wholesalers including Harrods, Selfridges and Mr Porter.
key_points: Derek Rose is marking 100 years in business, having been founded in 1926 by the grandfather of current chief executive Sacha Rose.
The new menswear collection is called 'As You Please' and includes knitwear made with Cariaggi in Italy, denim and cotton-cashmere trousers.
Prices run from £210 for cotton-cashmere lounge trousers to £775 for a wool and cashmere sweater, with a women's cashmere dressing gown at about £2,795.
Ready-to-wear and loungewear make up 70 per cent of sales, with pyjamas 30 per cent; around 80 per cent of the business is menswear.
The brand plans a website relaunch in the first quarter of 2027, an updated logo and more ready-to-wear, pursuing 'measured' growth.

stories.headline: CEO TALKS: Galeries Lafayette’s Arthur Lemoine on Luxury, Loyalty and That Christmas Tree
stories.claim: Galeries Lafayette CEO Arthur Lemoine says the department store is confident in Christmas despite protests and Middle East disruption.
stories.summary: Galeries Lafayette, the Paris department store group, reported 3.1 billion euros of revenue in 2025, with its Boulevard Haussmann flagship generating 2 billion euros, up 4 per cent. Chief executive Arthur Lemoine, who succeeded his cousin Nicolas Houzé, says the group is betting on stores as destinations rather than competing with online retail on convenience. Protests across France since 17 October have hit Saturday trade and deterred some international visitors, though the flagships have offset losses on other days. The beauty department has seen double-digit growth since its refurbishment, and a men's building is due for completion by the end of 2027.
key_points: Galeries Lafayette Group generated 3.1 billion euros in revenue in 2025, with the Haussmann flagship providing about two-thirds.
Protests that began on 17 October have hit Saturday sales and prompted some international visitors to cancel trips to France.
Lemoine says hotel and restaurant reservations have slowed, but it is too early to call an overall drop in tourist spending.
Beauty is growing at double digits since refurbishment, with new brands including Bottega Veneta and Victoria Beckham.
The men's building is expected to be finished by the end of 2027; its holiday tree designed by Jean-Charles de Castelbajac has drawn social media criticism.
stories.market_take: Galeries Lafayette is privately owned, so there is no direct share price impact.

stories.headline: Benefits review to suggest quicker payment for some disabled people
stories.claim: UK review of Personal Independence Payment (Pip) to recommend faster payments for severe cases, with no major savings expected.
stories.summary: A review of the UK's main disability benefit, Personal Independence Payment, is due to be published on Tuesday and will recommend faster payments for people with the most severe conditions and terminal illnesses. The Timms Review, chaired by Disability Minister Sir Stephen Timms, is expected to propose that payments be linked to real-life needs and extra costs rather than diagnosis. About one in ten claimants would be fast-tracked without reassessment. The government plans to spend £32.1bn on Pip this financial year, rising to £41.5bn by 2030-31, and the review is understood not to propose major savings. The proposals will go to a steering group, and the government will respond later.
key_points: The Timms Review is due to be published on Tuesday afternoon and is chaired by Sir Stephen Timms.
Around one in ten claimants with severe, persistent conditions would be fast-tracked without further assessments.
Pip spending is set at £32.1bn this year and is projected to reach £41.5bn in 2030-31.
The review is understood not to propose major cost savings, and reportedly will not introduce means-testing or vouchers.
Disability groups have broadly welcomed the proposals, while some think tanks want tighter eligibility for mental health claims.

stories.headline: Ascletis Announces Initiation of U.S. Phase I Study of ASC37i, a Potentially First-in-Class Once-Monthly to Once-Quarterly GLP-1R/GIPR/GCGR Triple Peptide Agonist, for the Treatment of Obesity – Company Announcement
stories.claim: Hong Kong-listed Ascletis has started a US Phase I trial of its once-monthly obesity drug ASC37i.
stories.summary: Ascletis Pharma, listed in Hong Kong under 1672, has begun a US Phase I trial of ASC37i, a once-monthly to once-quarterly obesity injection, after FDA clearance of its investigational new drug application. The triple peptide agonist targets the GLP-1, GIPR and GCGR receptors and is designed to be given by a thin-needle auto-injector. In mouse studies the company reports 88% greater relative weight loss than tirzepatide at the same dose, with up to 41.5% weight loss. In monkeys, the drug's half-life was about 17 days compared with 2.5 days for retatrutide. Because it is a biologic, it would face a longer exclusivity period under US rules. The data are preclinical and company-reported, and the trial is only at an early safety stage.
key_points: The US Phase I study of ASC37i has started after FDA clearance, in healthy adults with obesity or overweight.
The company reports 88% greater weight loss than tirzepatide in a diet-induced obese mouse study, though this is preclinical data.
Monkey studies show a half-life of about 17 days, roughly seven times longer than retatrutide.
As a biologic filed under a BLA, the drug would get 13 years of protection from price negotiations rather than nine.
stories.market_take: Positive read-across for the obesity-drug race, but early-stage data and a small Hong Kong listing mean limited near-term market effect.

stories.summary: Dior has appointed Nicole Orofino, formerly of L'Oréal, as global director of innovation for communication and image, effective immediately. stories.headline: Malaysia set to repatriate thousands more Myanmar migrants: PM
stories.claim: Malaysia will repatriate over 6,500 Myanmar migrants in December, including 1,500 by naval ship on 6-7 December.
stories.summary: Malaysia plans to send more than 6,500 Myanmar migrants back home in December, the largest announced round so far. Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim told parliament on Tuesday that three naval ships will carry 1,500 Myanmar citizens on 6 and 7 December, while 5,303 more will be flown back during the month at Myanmar's expense. The move follows a September scheme that returned around 1,500 people, which rights groups say may endanger migrants by sending them back to a war-torn country. The announcement comes five days after the International Court of Justice ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, and that Myanmar must allow refugees to return safely. Kuala Lumpur had earlier said it would seek clarification after hundreds of returnees were reportedly held in military detention.

stories.headline: Can Burnham turn volume down on EU debate?
stories.claim: Burnham declined to rule out a future in/out EU referendum and set out a calmer approach to UK-EU ties after the summit.
stories.summary: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has declined to rule out seeking a mandate for another EU referendum at the next general election, saying he would recommend one only if it served Britain's national interest. Speaking to the Commons after Friday's EU-UK summit in Brussels, he said there was 'no fixed destination' and promised no 'running commentary' on Europe. The government publishes its European Partnerships Bill on Thursday, with the legal text of the agreements due later in the week. Negotiations continue on university tuition fees for EU students, which both sides think is within reach within six months, and on the EU's common electricity market. Brussels is reportedly prepared to charge London for reinstating food export checkpoints if the UK reverses the food deal within ten years. The piece also notes the EU's willingness to include the UK in its 'Made in Europe' plan.
key_points: Burnham told MPs he would only recommend another EU referendum if it were in Britain's national interest.

stories.headline: Coldest spell of autumn continues with risk of hill snow, ice and heavy rain
stories.claim: The coldest spell of autumn brings hill snow, ice and heavy rain to parts of the UK this week, with a Met Office rain warning for Cornwall.
stories.summary: The coldest spell of the autumn so far is set to continue across the UK this week, bringing Arctic air to Scotland and northern and eastern England. Hill snow, freezing rain and ice are possible on high ground such as the Grampians and the North Pennines, while milder, wetter air brings heavy rain to south-west England, Wales and Northern Ireland. The Met Office has issued a yellow warning for rain covering Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly from 10:00 GMT on Tuesday, with 30-40mm widely and up to 60-90mm possible in western Cornwall. Wednesday brings fog or freezing fog, mostly in Northern Ireland, before colder but mostly dry weather returns on Friday. Localised flooding and difficult driving conditions are possible.
key_points: Arctic air is bringing below-average temperatures and wintry hazards to Scotland and northern and eastern England.

stories.headline: Solomon Islands plans to replace China security pact with Australia treaty, report says
stories.claim: Solomon Islands reportedly will end its 2022 China security pact and sign a new Australia treaty as its top security partner.
stories.summary: The Solomon Islands has reportedly told China it will not renew its five-year security agreement signed in 2022, which expires in April, according to the Sydney Morning Herald. The report says Australia and the Solomon Islands are expected to sign a comprehensive treaty making Canberra the Pacific nation's top security partner when Prime Minister Matthew Wale meets Anthony Albanese on Wednesday. The strategic islands sit about 1,600 km northeast of Australia, and Beijing's growing influence in the Pacific has been a major concern for Canberra and Washington. Voters' worries about ties with China helped bring Wale to power in May.

stories.headline: Paolo Bulgari, third-generation head of Bulgari jewellery dynasty, dies at 89
stories.claim: Paolo Bulgari, long-serving chairman of the Italian jewellery house Bulgari, has died in Rome aged 89.
stories.summary: Paolo Bulgari, a member of the family behind the Italian jewellery house Bulgari and a key figure in its growth into a global luxury brand, has died in Rome aged 89. His family announced the death on Saturday 21 November 2026, calling him the greatest jeweller of his time. He joined the family business in 1960 and became chairman in 1984, a post he held alongside his brother Nicola. Under the family, the house expanded into watches, which came to account for around 40 per cent of revenues, as well as perfumes and accessories, and he helped popularise coloured gemstones. Bulgari listed in Milan in 1995 and the family sold its controlling stake to LVMH in 2011 for about €3.7 billion, a move the family called painful but necessary. The family was acquitted of tax evasion charges in 2015, and in 2019 he founded the Paolo Bulgari Foundation with his wife to support education in disadvantaged parts of Rome.

stories.headline: Malaysian govt did not leak minutes of Pardons Board meeting on Najib: Anwar
stories.claim: Anwar Ibrahim says the Malaysian government did not leak the Pardons Board minutes on Najib Razak.
stories.summary: Malaysia's Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim has told parliament that his government did not leak the minutes of the Pardons Board meeting on jailed former prime minister Najib Razak. He said neither the Legal Affairs Division nor the Attorney-General's Chambers circulated the document, and that the Home Ministry should investigate how it came to be published prematurely. Anwar argued that the Attorney-General had simply prepared a response to a court application, and that only the board's decision, not its minutes, had been requested. Lawmaker Ahmad Fadhli Shaari questioned whether the Official Secrets Act required declassification and why a third party had made the document public first. The row touches on Cabinet confidentiality and Najib's continuing legal battles.
key_points: Anwar told the Dewan Rakyat on Nov 24 that the government did not circulate the Pardons Board minutes on Najib Razak.

stories.headline: Mexico captures FBI most-wanted cartel boss 'El Chapo Isidro'; can it dismantle his cartel?
stories.claim: Mexican forces captured cartel boss 'El Chapo Isidro' in a raid in Sinaloa; analysts question whether the cartel can be dismantled.
stories.summary: Mexico's military captured Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as 'El Chapo Isidro' and one of the FBI's 10 most wanted fugitives, in a special forces raid in Guasave, Sinaloa, on Friday night. The operation, which Mexico's defence ministry said had US intelligence support, triggered gunfights, burning vehicles and roadblocks across Sinaloa, easing by Saturday. Two other alleged gang leaders, including his second-in-command, were arrested with him and flown to Mexico City for prosecutors. Security forces said seven attackers were killed, eight suspects were arrested and four Mexican soldiers died. Meza Flores was indicted in the US in 2012, carries a US$5m reward, and is accused of trafficking heroin, methamphetamine, cocaine and fentanyl. The capture is a significant blow to the Beltrán Leyva group, though a follow-up analysis notes that cartels remain deeply embedded in Mexican politics and the economy.

stories.headline: US Army to detonate about five tonnes of toxic lead azide in Iowa after court clears plan
stories.claim: US Army to detonate about five tonnes of lead azide at Iowa Army Ammunition Plant on Wednesday after appeals court clears the plan.
stories.summary: The US Army is set to detonate about five tonnes of degraded lead azide, a volatile compound, at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown on Wednesday morning. The 8th Circuit Court of Appeals declined on Monday to block the operation, finding an emergency and adequate safeguards in place. The detonation has already been postponed three times, and President Trump had earlier paused it until courts and incoming Democratic governor Rob Sand agreed. Sand has not said whether he supports the move, while the current governor, Kim Reynolds, backs it. Environmental groups, including the Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club, warned of a plume of toxic lead particles and accused the government of bypassing the courts, arguing the EPA had not weighed the risks. The EPA issued an emergency permit covering 68 drums, citing an imminent threat to health and the environment. Officials say the material has degraded and that cold weather raises the risk of an uncontrolled explosion, which is why they consider it too unstable to store.
key_points: The Army will detonate about five tonnes (around 9,500 pounds) of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown on Wednesday morning.

The story highlights weak oversight of dog licensing in England, where there is no official register of breeders and star ratings.

stories.headline: US blacklists Singapore-based Megaspeed and six firms over alleged Nvidia chip diversion
stories.claim: The US Commerce Department added Singapore-based Megaspeed and six other Southeast Asian firms to its Entity List, requiring licences for advanced US chips.
stories.summary: The US Commerce Department added Singapore-based Megaspeed International and six other Southeast Asian firms to its Entity List on Monday 23 November, the same day Jensen Huang returned as Nvidia chief executive. Listed firms now need a US licence to receive advanced American technology, including Nvidia's top AI GPUs, and applications are likely to be denied. The department said it suspected Megaspeed of routing Nvidia chips to Chinese companies in breach of export controls after almost two years of investigation. Three of the listed companies are in Malaysia, one in Thailand and two in Singapore. Singapore's prime minister Lawrence Wong said his government is working with Washington on an enforcement mechanism, while saying Singapore lacks full information on chip end users. Malaysia's trade ministry will advise data centre operators not to host or serve the blacklisted firms, though this is advice rather than a ban. China has warned against a technological blockade.

stories.headline: Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO after Trump push; shares surge
stories.claim: Nvidia's board unanimously reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO and president on 23 November, after US government input and Trump's push; shares surged about 30%.
stories.summary: Nvidia's board unanimously reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive and president with immediate effect on Monday 23 November, less than two weeks after he resigned, saying US government input indicated his return poses no national security risk. Nvidia shares jumped roughly 30 per cent at the open, adding close to $1tn in market value and lifting the Nasdaq and Dow sharply. The reversal followed a campaign in which President Trump said he 'made the deal' by pressing the board, including by phone during a board meeting, and JD Vance reportedly reassured directors. Huang had stepped down on 12 November after admitting an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, a Singapore-based executive whom US intelligence has reportedly linked to a Chinese espionage network, and he was also reported to have had an affair with an Nvidia executive. Colette Kress, who served as interim CEO, will remain chief financial officer. Bipartisan lawmakers, including Senator Elizabeth Warren, have demanded answers, while the SEC and Department of Justice investigations and an independent board probe into security and intellectual property leakage continue. The episode underscores how closely investors and policymakers watch Nvidia, the world's most valuable chipmaker.
key_points: Nvidia's board unanimously reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive, president and director with immediate effect on 23 November.
The board said US government input indicated his return poses no national security risk and that it was satisfied with his candour and ability to lead.
Nvidia shares closed about 31 per cent higher, adding nearly $1tn in market value, while the Nasdaq rose about 6.4 per cent.
Trump said he 'made the deal' and pressed the board, and reports say VP JD Vance held a private call with Huang and reassured directors.
Huang resigned on 12 November after admitting an affair with Alice Huang, whom US intelligence has reportedly linked to China, and a second affair reportedly involving an Nvidia executive.
Colette Kress remains CFO, while the SEC, Department of Justice and an independent board probe continue, and Senator Warren demanded answers from Huang and Nvidia.
stories.market_take: Investors see Huang's return as a sign of continuity for Nvidia, which is a bellwether for the AI chip trade.

stories.headline: UN food agency chief warns wars jeopardize food aid for 7.3 million more people
stories.claim: WFP warns wars and shipping chokepoints could add $727m to its costs and threaten food for 7.3 million more people.
stories.summary: The World Food Programme warned the UN Security Council that shipping disruption tied to wars in the Middle East and Ukraine could add $727 million to its costs by mid-2027. That shortfall could put food aid at risk for 7.3 million more people. Executive Director Luke Lindberg said constraints through the Strait of Hormuz, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the Black Sea, combined with El Niño, were making the situation worse. He called for a Black Sea corridor modelled on the 2022 UN-brokered grain initiative, which Russia quit in 2023. Black Sea wheat and maize shipments through the Bosphorus were down 63% by mid-October compared with 2025, with over 300 attacks recorded and at least 40 crew killed. Lindberg also noted 266 million people face acute hunger, with famine risks in Sudan, South Sudan and Somalia.

This could threaten food aid for 7.3 million more people.
Black Sea wheat and maize vessel traffic through the Bosphorus was down 63% by mid-October versus 2025.
Over 300 attacks and at least 40 crew deaths were recorded in the Black Sea, according to Lindberg.
He urged a revived Black Sea grain corridor covering both Russian and Ukrainian exports.
266 million people face acute hunger globally, with famine risks in Sudan, South Sudan and Somalia.

stories.headline: Amazon buys AI accelerator technology and staff from Israeli startup Decart
stories.claim: Amazon has agreed to acquire Decart's AI optimisation technology and its founders and engineers in a deal Bloomberg values at about $7.5bn; neither company has confirmed a price.
stories.summary: Amazon has agreed to acquire the proprietary AI optimisation technology of Israeli startup Decart, along with its three founders and engineering team, in a deal Bloomberg reports is valued at around $7.5 billion. The move follows earlier reports, from November, that Amazon was closing in on a deal of about $7.5bn including cash, stock and performance earnouts, with the Wall Street Journal first reporting talks around $7bn in October. Amazon describes the deal as an asset purchase rather than a whole-company takeover, so Decart's other models are not included and the startup's future is unclear. Neither company has disclosed a price. The Decart Optimization Stack sits between AI models and chips, tuning kernels, compilers and runtimes so accelerators stay fully utilised, and it supports Nvidia GPUs, Google TPUs and AWS Trainium chips. Amazon SVP Peter DeSantis framed the deal as a way to push Trainium and its AI efforts further. If the Bloomberg figure holds, it would rank among Amazon's largest acquisitions, behind its $8.5 billion purchase of MGM. The deal underlines Amazon's push to cut inference costs and make its own chips more competitive. Decart raised $300m in May 2026 at roughly a $4bn valuation.

stories.headline: DeepMind’s AI agents found cheaper quantum algorithms, and proved them
stories.claim: Google DeepMind agent teams found much cheaper quantum algorithms for fusion, chemistry and drug design, with results proved in Lean.
stories.summary: Google DeepMind and Google Quantum AI say teams of Gemini 4 agents have found quantum algorithms that are far cheaper to run for fusion, chemistry and drug-design problems, and proved each result correct in the Lean theorem prover. The biggest gain is a laser-driven fusion fuel calculation that becomes 11.8 times cheaper, with error-corrected qubit needs falling from 5,650 to 4,338. A simulation of a light-sensitive molecule is about eight times cheaper, the cost of simulating Cytochrome P450, an enzyme that breaks down most medicines, falls 2.5 times, and a widely used maths routine becomes more than 290 times cheaper. The circuits are too large to test on today's machines, which is why formal proofs were used, and an outside checker re-ran every proof to rule out gaming. DeepMind cautions the workloads will still need far more resources than the first error-corrected quantum computers will offer, and has open-sourced its Lean library and results.
key_points: DeepMind and Google Quantum AI used teams of Gemini 4 agents to find cheaper quantum algorithms.
The fusion fuel calculation became 11.8 times cheaper, with qubit needs cut from 5,650 to 4,338.
Cytochrome P450 simulation cost fell 2.5 times; a light-sensitive molecule simulation is about eight times cheaper.
Every result was proved in Lean and re-checked by an outside party, since the circuits are too large to test directly.
DeepMind says the simulations still need far more resources than early error-corrected machines will provide, and has open-sourced its work.

stories.headline: Channel 4 hit as Unilever switches from TV to influencer marketing
stories.claim: Unilever has shifted marketing money toward influencers, hurting TV broadcasters such as ITV, Sky and Channel 4.
stories.summary: Unilever has expanded its creator network from 75,000 in 2024 to more than 500,000, and its spending is moving away from traditional broadcasters. Guardian analysis finds ITV and Sky's sales operations saw bigger declines in Unilever spend than Channel 4, which is the biggest loser relative to its size. Unilever's chief marketing officer says creator-led content delivers 1.5 times the return on investment of branded content. Thinkbox, the UK TV marketing body, counters that TV generated 39% of campaign awareness uplift versus 1% for influencers. Unilever says AI tools let it produce 12 times more content while cutting production costs by 90%. The shift matters because Unilever's marketing budget exceeds €8bn, and it is also combining its food business with McCormick in a $44.8bn deal expected to complete in mid-2027.

Unilever's marketing budget is above €8bn (£6.7bn) and about 70% now goes on digital channels.

It arrives after enterprise pushback over the 30-day data retention Anthropic introduced when it launched Fable 5. Under EFS, prompts and replies sit in the customer's own Amazon or Google cloud account, encrypted so that not even the customer can read them, and nobody at Anthropic or the cloud provider sees them. When the system flags a risk, the customer's security team has seven days to investigate or risk losing access. More than 100 customers helped build it, including Bridgewater, Salesforce and Stripe, and Wells Fargo has publicly backed the approach. The system is free, though customers pay their cloud provider for storage, and it follows OpenAI's similar Private Safety Processing preview in August.

stories.headline: Germany warns Russia could put nuclear weapon in space within 60 days; NATO vows defence
stories.claim: Germany says it takes seriously intelligence reports that Russia could launch a nuclear-armed satellite, Sputnik-S, within 60 days; NATO vows defence, Kremlin denies.
stories.summary: NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte pledged to defend alliance territory in space after German broadcasters NDR and WDR and the Süddeutsche Zeitung reported that Russia could launch a nuclear-armed satellite, named Sputnik-S, within 60 days. Germany said it was taking the intelligence-based reports very seriously, and Chancellor Friedrich Merz, speaking alongside Rutte, said they showed the escalation Russia was prepared to pursue. The reports cite Western intelligence that the satellite was assembled years ago and sits near Moscow, with warnings in early November that a launch could come within that window. The Kremlin called the claims speculative and said it had not seen the report, while the Russian embassy in Berlin called them unfounded propaganda. Berlin has not confirmed the reports, and no official confirmation has been published. stories.headline: Why Amazon’s Rival to Starlink Is Struggling to Catch Up With SpaceX
stories.claim: Amazon's Leo satellite internet is falling behind SpaceX's Starlink after launch partner setbacks grounded its rockets.
stories.summary: Amazon's Leo satellite internet service is struggling to keep pace with SpaceX's Starlink, with only around 396 satellites launched to date against more than 11,000 Starlink satellites in operation. Amazon's last successful Leo deployment was 12 weeks ago, on 2 July, aboard a ULA Atlas V rocket. Its main alternatives are grounded: ULA's Vulcan has been out since February after a booster anomaly, and Blue Origin's New Glenn has been down since its only launchpad was destroyed in May. Amazon has also ordered more Ariane 6 launches, but a component issue is expected to disrupt them for the rest of 2026. The FCC has extended Amazon's deadline to launch half of its planned 3,232 satellites, on condition that it moves quickly. SpaceX is meanwhile preparing to launch its first Starlink V3 satellites on Starship.

stories.headline: OpenAI chief scientist proposes industry-wide limits on powerful AI until safety monitoring improves

stories.summary: OpenAI's chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, has called on AI developers to agree common limits on building increasingly powerful models until researchers can better understand and monitor them. In a blog post published on Sunday, 22 November, he suggested shared thresholds based partly on perplexity, a measure of how well a model predicts text, with developers committing not to cross them until monitoring and safety milestones are reached. He did not specify an initial limit or a start date, and warned that AI could drive fundamental training advances as early as 2027, potentially outpacing safety work. CEO Sam Altman endorsed the idea on X, calling it the most important thing OpenAI has published in a while. The proposal is voluntary rather than regulation, and it lands as US Democrats, who won sweeping midterm victories, prepare to push for tougher AI oversight, setting up a likely clash with President Trump, who has opposed broad AI restrictions.

stories.headline: Former PMs May, Cameron and Blair warn Andy Burnham against rejoining EU
stories.claim: Former PMs Theresa May and Tony Blair have warned Prime Minister Andy Burnham against rejoining the EU after his Brussels 'reset deal'.
stories.summary: Former prime ministers are warning Andy Burnham against seeking to rejoin the European Union. Theresa May told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that she was 'aghast' he is considering it, saying 'Brexit is done' and that he wanted to 'pat people on the head'. Tony Blair said Britain should rejoin only if the EU reforms and embraces technology and innovation, calling Brexit 'a real mistake', while David Cameron said a rejoin conversation would be long and painful. Four of Britain's nine living ex-PMs have now spoken out. The comments follow Burnham's 'reset deal' struck at a Brussels summit on Friday, which gives 100,000 Europeans aged 18 to 31 the right to live, work and study in Britain for up to three years, aligns Britain with EU food and drink safety rules and links emissions trading. Burnham has floated the customs union, single market or a fresh referendum for informal long-term talks, but has ruled out major changes before the next general election, citing Labour's 2024 manifesto. Reform UK called the deal a betrayal, while Kemi Badenoch plans to attack it at a CBI speech and in parliament on Monday.

stories.headline: Russian strikes kill at least nine in Dymer, Ukraine; boy rescued alive from rubble
stories.claim: Russian strikes killed at least ten people in Dymer, Ukraine, and a seven-year-old boy was pulled alive from rubble after about 14 hours.
stories.summary: Rescuers in Ukraine pulled a seven-year-old boy alive from the rubble of a residential building in Dymer, north of Kyiv, after about 14 hours of work following a Russian strike. Ukrainian officials say the overnight attacks killed ten people in Dymer, and a 79-year-old woman was also rescued alive, while more than 130 emergency workers are at the scene. Zelensky described the five-storey block as largely destroyed. Across the Kyiv region and beyond, strikes killed one in Bila Tserkva and three in a Vyshneve grocery store, where 13 were wounded, and Ukraine's interior minister said more than 70 strikes were launched across 10 regions by Sunday evening. Russia also struck a power substation in the Dnipropetrovsk region. Separately, a Russian navy corvette, the Merkury, was severely damaged and sank in the Libyan port of Benghazi in a suspected Ukrainian sea drone attack, more than 1,000 miles from Ukraine, though no one has claimed responsibility. In Poland, prosecutors identified three objects that landed on Friday as Russian Kh-101 cruise missiles, with no injuries; Nato allies meet in Brussels on Monday, and Tusk called the incident an intentional provocation. Denmark has expelled a Russian official over an alleged plot against a Ukrainian American rapper.

stories.headline: Democrats win largest US House majority since 1992, with about 259 seats
stories.claim: Democrats win their largest US House majority since 1992, with at least 258 seats after Chuck Hubbard unseated Virginia Foxx.
stories.summary: Democrats have secured their largest majority in the US House since 1992, with CNN projecting 259 seats in the 435-member chamber. The party reached at least 258 seats on Sunday after Democrat Chuck Hubbard beat Republican incumbent Virginia Foxx by 330 votes in North Carolina's 5th district. Foxx, who had held the seat since 2005, requested a recount under state law and then conceded. Republicans hold at least 173 seats, with four races still uncalled, including contests in Minnesota and Tennessee, and two Louisiana seats heading to a 12 December runoff. The party's net gain of around 40 to 44 seats would be the third-largest in half a century, behind 2010 and 1994. Democrats also control the Senate with a 56-seat majority, creating divided government under President Donald Trump. Voters cited high prices, the war with Iran and corruption concerns. Democrats plan a 100-day agenda from January on living costs, healthcare and immigration, including investigating the administration and blocking cabinet nominees, though Trump retains veto power.

stories.headline: Dutch court bars BYD Ti7 SUV from EU sales over Land Rover Defender design copy
stories.claim: A Dutch court has banned BYD's Ti7 SUV from EU sales in a ruling for Jaguar Land Rover over its Defender design, and BYD says it will appeal.
stories.summary: A district court in The Hague has banned Chinese carmaker BYD from selling its Ti7 SUV in the European Union, ruling in summary proceedings that the vehicle infringes Jaguar Land Rover's EU design rights. The ban takes effect one week after the Friday 20 November ruling and also halts production at BYD's planned Szeged factory in Hungary until the case is resolved. The court said it lacked jurisdiction over BYD's UK activities, where the Ti7 is priced at £47,995 with deliveries from January 2027 and is not affected. BYD says it strongly disagrees, calls the design its own independent work, and plans to appeal, while the court noted BYD has no concrete EU sales plans. The case was brought by JLR, which argued the boxy SUV was a 'Defender clone'; the Defender's starting price is just under £72,000, and JLR sold 29,500 Defenders to retail customers in July to September. The ruling is a rare European court test of copycat design claims against a Chinese carmaker, and BYD's shares were reported to have fallen.

stories.headline: COP31 talks in Antalya collapse over fossil fuel language; draft omits coal, oil and gas
stories.claim: COP31 talks in Antalya collapsed on Monday after more than two weeks of deadlock over fossil fuel and climate finance language.
stories.summary: The COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, collapsed on Monday after more than two weeks of contentious talks, making it the longest-ever UN climate negotiations, with countries unable to agree on fossil fuels or on money. Earlier, on the Sunday of overtime talks, the latest draft from the Turkish and Australian presidency again avoided naming coal, oil or gas, instead referring to the 2023 Dubai consensus on moving away from fossil fuels. About 130 countries, backed by the EU, wanted explicit transition language, while Saudi Arabia and other oil-rich states opposed it, and the EU raised the prospect of 'no deal'. Tuvalu's climate minister called the fossil fuel reference a red line. Other disputes included carbon capture and storage and a target for electricity to reach 35% of final energy by 2035. Developing nations objected to the removal of a US$120 billion climate adaptation target, and some delegates left, raising quorum concerns. Campaigners called it the 'worst COP ever', pointing to Berkeley Earth's finding that October 2026 was the warmest October on record. The breakdown undermines the idea of broad consensus on phasing out fossil fuels, a key goal of global climate diplomacy.
key_points: The longest-ever UN climate negotiations, COP31 in Antalya, collapsed on Monday without agreement on fossil fuels or climate finance.
The talks had been scheduled to end on Friday and ran into days of overtime.

Democrats, who take control of Congress in January, have promised oversight of ICE tactics, adding pressure to the Trump administration's immigration crackdown.

stories.headline: Lean verifies Anthropic claim that Claude helped prove the Riemann hypothesis
stories.claim: Lean FRO and Mathlib Initiative say they independently verified the Lean code behind Anthropic's claimed Riemann hypothesis proof, though the proof is not yet accepted.
stories.summary: The Lean Focused Research Organization and the Mathlib Initiative said on Saturday they had independently verified a proof of the Riemann hypothesis by checking the Lean code published by Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge, and expressed full confidence in its correctness. Alpöge, who said he worked with a non-public version of Claude over about six weeks, first made the claim on Friday, a day after Anthropic's record Nasdaq debut, and acknowledged the timing was awkward. Several Zulip participants, including Andrew Sutherland of MIT, said the code compiles, though Terence Tao said human verification will take time. The complete argument reportedly runs to more than 250,000 pages and lacks a readable human explanation. Under Clay Institute rules a solution needs peer review and two years of scrutiny before the $1 million prize is paid, and Stanford's Ravi Vakil had earlier posted a human-written draft of the Generalised Riemann Hypothesis that was later flagged for problems.

stories.headline: Israel’s destruction of Gaza has created a ‘toxic wasteland’, experts find
stories.claim: An Oxfam and Ceobs report finds widespread toxic contamination across Gaza from Israel's military assault, threatening long-term public health.
stories.summary: A new report by Oxfam and the Conflict and Environment Observatory describes Gaza as a 'toxic wasteland' after Israel's military campaign, with heavy metals, explosive residues, asbestos and sewage contaminating air, soil and water across the entire strip. The UN Environment Programme estimates more than 61 million tonnes of debris have been generated, and unexploded ordnance limits safe access to most areas. Israel's mission in Geneva has rejected the UN commission's findings, and the Israeli government has not yet responded to the report.

stories.claim: The US war with Iran has settled into a low-level, protracted conflict after talks were dropped in favour of a blockade.
stories.summary: Roughly ten months into the US war with Iran, Washington has abandoned negotiations in favour of a naval blockade, and analysts expect a long, low-level conflict. Recent flare-ups include a gas tanker hit in the Strait of Hormuz, a US strike on a missile site on Qeshm Island and Iranian drones fired at Bahrain and Kuwait. US petrol is about $3.70 a gallon, up from just under $3 before the war, and the Pentagon puts the war's cost near $50bn. The war keeps energy markets and the Gulf region on edge.

stories.headline: Judge Blocks Trump Administration’s Effort to Transform Homelessness Policy
stories.claim: US judge blocks Trump administration's overhaul of a roughly $4bn homelessness programme, ordering new grant plan.
stories.summary: A federal judge in Rhode Island has blocked the Trump administration's latest attempt to shift housing aid toward treatment-first programmes, ruling it exceeded its statutory authority. The administration wanted to redirect about $1.3 billion, roughly a third of a $4 billion annual homelessness grant pot, from permanent supportive housing to programmes requiring mental health or addiction treatment. Judge Mary S. McElroy ruled it was the third time she has stopped the government rewriting these grantmaking rules, and she gave the Department of Housing and Urban Development five days to submit a new disbursement plan. Advocates say around 97,000 formerly homeless people could have lost housing under the change, while HUD Secretary Scott Turner said the ruling disrupts funding for the most vulnerable and did not say whether an appeal would follow. The fight is a wider battle over the Housing First model, which has bipartisan roots but is now criticised for its cost and limited evidence on health outcomes.

stories.headline: UN Geneva talks fail to agree binding rules on killer robots, deferring to 2028
stories.claim: UN Geneva talks on killer robots ended without a binding treaty mandate, deferring work on an instrument to a 2028 meeting.
stories.summary: UN talks in Geneva on lethal autonomous weapons collapsed at about 5am on Saturday without a mandate for a legally binding treaty. All 128 states under the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons agreed instead to develop an international instrument over two years, reporting to a 2028 meeting. Russia objected to the agenda on the first day and blocked formal negotiations, and under the consensus rule its objections shaped a much weaker outcome. The US, UK, France, Germany, Japan, South Korea, Turkey and Israel were named by EU diplomats as resisting binding rules, with the US proposing a five-year window for non-binding guidelines. More than 100 states had wanted a new law, and a bloc led by Austria, Belgium, Brazil, Ireland, Mexico, New Zealand and Panama pushed for a treaty within a year. The International Committee of the Red Cross and UN chief António Guterres want a binding instrument, and campaigners called the result a missed opportunity, warning that it may soon be too late to regulate such weapons.

stories.claim: Poundland could collapse into administration despite improved trading, as owner Gordon Brothers restricts cash and weighs a break-up.

Its US owner, Gordon Brothers, which bought the chain for £1 from Pepco, put the business up for sale in September and has rejected offers, including a Martin Property Group bid that would have protected jobs. Gordon Brothers froze about £50m of cash before releasing around £21m over two weeks, and it is weighing a break-up, which it says would better protect staff. Insiders accuse it of driving the business down for insolvency gains, which it denies. Trading has improved: first-quarter like-for-like sales rose 7%, Halloween sales were 11.4% higher than a year earlier, and the year to September moved to an £18.1m profit before interest, tax and certain charges from a £68m loss. Xyra Group has made a rescue bid, though its credibility is doubted, and the deadline for a rescue deal has been extended by 10 days. Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds have pressed Gordon Brothers for answers.

stories.claim: Delta flights at Atlanta's Hartsfield-Jackson airport and nationwide were delayed Sunday after its weight-and-balance system failed.
stories.summary: Delta Air Lines flights at Atlanta's Hartsfield-Jackson airport, its largest hub, faced significant delays on Sunday after its system for calculating aircraft weight, centre of gravity and load distribution went offline. Staff used manual workarounds to dispatch aircraft while technicians restored the system, and the disruption reached flights across the US. The FAA said the Delta problem was unrelated to its own air traffic control systems. The incident comes a week after an FAA telecoms failure on 13 November caused a nationwide ground stop of over four hours and about 12,462 cancellations; the agency linked that outage to a router installation at a facility run by L3Harris and paused further installations. United Airlines also delayed departures after a separate outage of its own. The incidents do not share a single confirmed cause, but they have raised questions about the reliability of US aviation infrastructure, and knock-on delays to other carriers are possible if the problem persists.

stories.claim: A drone strike set the Russian cargo ship Sparta II ablaze in the Gulf of Finland, and Finland says Ukraine was likely responsible.
stories.summary: A Russian cargo ship, the Sparta II, was set ablaze in the Gulf of Finland on Saturday after being hit by drones, and it later drifted into Finnish waters. Finland's armed forces and Border Guard point to Ukraine as likely responsible, though Kyiv has not commented and the reason for the attack is unclear. The vessel, bound for the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, was sanctioned by the US and Ukraine and is reportedly suspected of carrying weapons from Syria to Russia. All 16 crew abandoned ship in lifeboats and were transferred to a nearby Russian vessel that is taking them home. Finland's defence minister said a Russian helicopter may have violated Finnish airspace during the rescue, and Helsinki introduced temporary aviation and maritime restrictions in the eastern Gulf. Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said the war was spilling into the region, and the episode comes as Russian missiles and a drone crashed in Poland and NATO is due to meet in Brussels on Monday.

stories.headline: Can AI spot breast cancer earlier? NHS launches world's largest trial to find out
stories.claim: NHS launches a 700,000-woman trial testing whether AI can help read breast cancer screening mammograms.
stories.summary: Nearly 700,000 women across the UK are being invited into what is described as the world's largest trial of artificial intelligence in breast cancer screening. The EDITH trial has started at Cambridge University Hospitals, the first of 30 NHS sites, and will run for around three years. Today two NHS specialists read each mammogram; in the trial one of those human readers will be replaced by AI, with AI either grading images before or reviewing them after experts see them. The £11m study is funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research and led by Warwick and Cambridge with NHS England, with four AI companies involved. Researchers say smaller studies show AI can raise detection rates, but they must confirm it does not cause unnecessary recalls or over-diagnosis of mild disease. Health Secretary Yvette Cooper backed the trial, saying safeguards are needed.
key_points: The EDITH trial will invite nearly 700,000 women aged 50 to 71 across the UK to take part in AI-assisted breast screening research.
Recruitment has begun at Cambridge University Hospitals, the first of 30 sites, and the study is expected to last about three years.
In one trial arm AI grades mammograms before human experts review them; in the other it reviews them afterwards.

Researchers want to ensure AI does not increase unnecessary recalls or diagnose mild cancers that would never cause symptoms.
Breast cancer causes around 59,000 UK diagnoses a year, and the screening programme is estimated to prevent about 1,300 deaths annually.

According to the Financial Times, Dell, HPE, Lenovo and Supermicro are passing on sharply higher memory costs, with demands arriving as equipment is ready for delivery. JPMorgan research cited by the paper puts memory-cost increases above 400% since early 2024. One person quoted said GPU-server prices rose at least 20–30%, while CPU-node prices tripled or more. stories.headline: South Asian nations emerge as labour sources for Japan’s ageing farms
stories.claim: Bangladeshi workers are emerging as a new labour source for Japan's ageing farms as South-east Asian wages rise.
stories.summary: Bangladesh and Nepal are becoming an important source of farm labour for Japan, as wages rise in Vietnam and the Philippines and the flow of workers from those countries slows. Tokyo-based training firm Mirai, part of Sustainable Holdings, has placed its first two Bangladeshi candidates for farm work, with jobs at an agricultural company in Aomori prefecture. Japanese government data show Type 1 specified skilled foreign workers in agriculture rose 26% year on year to 44,050 in June. Indonesia remains the largest supplier with 18,255 workers, while Bangladesh's numbers jumped 127% to 334. The shift matters because farm labour shortages in Japan are chronic, driven by an ageing population.

Wages rising in Vietnam, the Philippines and other South-east Asian countries are making those workers harder to attract.
Including Type 2 workers, the total in agriculture was 67,905 at the end of December 2025.
Sustainable Holdings offers free tuition at partner schools and helps with housing once workers arrive in Japan.

The agency links the growing risk to climate change, which is bringing more intense rainfall and rising sea levels.

stories.headline: What Comes Next After Anthropic’s Historic IPO
stories.claim: Anthropic raised a record $81bn in its US IPO and closed its first day of trading at about $1.7tn valuation.
stories.summary: Anthropic, the maker of the Claude chatbot, closed its first day of public trading about 17% above its IPO price, valuing the company at roughly $1.7tn at a share price just over $97. Assembly will now start in early January 2027 instead of December, with first deliveries expected at the end of January. The cause is a shortage of specialised fibreglass cloth for the phone's 12-layer printed circuit board, with only six suppliers worldwide and four unable to meet volume. stories.headline: Taiwan widens its short-selling ban after the Taiex’s worst week since 1991
stories.claim: Taiwan bans short selling below previous close and tightens margin rules after Taiex's worst week since 1991.
stories.summary: Taiwan's financial regulator has banned short selling of local stocks below the previous day's close, effective 23 November, after the Taiex suffered its worst week since 1991. The index fell 6.2% on Friday and lost almost 18% over the week. The Financial Supervisory Commission also raised the minimum margin for short sales to 150% from 130% and halted new put warrant listings. It is the third round of curbs this month, following earlier cuts to intraday short-selling limits and a ban for stocks that had fallen 3.5% or more. The sell-off has been driven by doubts over AI spending returns, worries about tighter US AI regulation and margin-financing risks, and the state-backed NT$500bn fund has been buying shares since 6 November.

Some analysts estimate Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet, Nvidia and Meta could spend as much as $1.4 trillion by 2027, while Gartner projects global AI spending will reach $2.5 trillion this year. stories.headline: Blair says UK should rejoin EU only if it reforms, especially on technology
stories.claim: Blair says the UK should rejoin the EU only on heavily conditioned terms, with EU reform and stronger UK tech innovation.
stories.summary: Sir Tony Blair has said Britain should rejoin the European Union only on heavily conditioned terms, arguing that the EU must reform and that Britain must be ready to walk away from talks. Speaking to The Sunday Times, he said Brexit was a real mistake but that the debate has changed since 2016, with technology innovation now central to the question. He warned that AI carries very considerable risks, that the EU may be moving in the wrong direction on tech, and that the UK lacks the dynamism of other countries in the sector. His remarks follow a deal Prime Minister Andy Burnham agreed with Brussels, which he described as a win-win reset covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme. A digital partnership on AI and quantum technology was also announced, with Ursula von der Leyen publicising it. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch called the deal unfair, while Reform's Nigel Farage called it a betrayal of the British people. Burnham has ruled out discussing rejoining, and both sides plan an informal process on long-term options before the next UK-EU summit.

stories.headline: Barnham villagers vote 94% to 'leave the UK' in symbolic poll against asylum plan
stories.claim: Residents of Barnham, Suffolk, voted 94% in a symbolic, non-binding poll to 'leave the UK' over plans to house asylum seekers at RAF Barnham.
stories.summary: Residents of the Suffolk village of Barnham voted 257 to 16 in a symbolic, non-binding poll on Saturday, with 94% of participants backing leaving the UK in protest at government plans to house up to 931 single male asylum seekers at the former RAF Barnham site. The vote has no legal force, as there is no mechanism for a village to leave the UK, and the village plans to call itself the 'Bailiwick of Barnham' and has unveiled its own flag. The Home Office has awarded a £3.4m design contract to Kier for the site, which could use a fast-track planning route, but said no final decision has been taken and that it is listening to local concerns. The council estimated around 500 people could vote, as it cannot use the electoral register. Barnham is the second village after Piddington in Oxfordshire to hold such a poll, where 285 of 312 voters backed leaving in September. Reform UK's Zia Yusuf attended the result, and Barnham's Labour MP Peter Prinsley said he will raise the opposition with the immigration minister this week. The plans are part of the government's effort to end hotel use for asylum seekers by 2029.

stories.headline: BepiColombo spacecraft enter orbit around Mercury despite thruster glitch
stories.claim: BepiColombo entered orbit around Mercury, but a software glitch cut short a key thruster burn; ESA says the mission remains on track.
stories.summary: Europe's and Japan's joint BepiColombo mission has entered orbit around Mercury, becoming only the third spacecraft to visit the planet and the second to orbit it. The European Space Agency said on Monday that the mission remains on track and the spacecraft is in a stable orbit, despite a software glitch that cut short a key thruster burn. The 37-minute burn, begun about 635 km above the surface, was interrupted early, so the craft achieved roughly 77% of the planned velocity change, and it entered safe mode for a time. The spacecraft had travelled more than eight years and about 6bn miles to reach Mercury. Further thruster burns are scheduled in coming months to adjust the orbit. The two orbiters are still due to separate on 9 December, with one European and one Japanese craft. Routine science operations are expected to begin in April, and the orbiters should last about three years. The €1.6bn mission aims to explain how Mercury formed so close to the Sun, why it has a magnetic field, and what ice lies in its permanently shadowed craters.

stories.headline: Anthropic shares slip after record IPO as AI-led tech rout pushes US indexes into correction
stories.claim: US indexes entered correction as an AI-led tech rout hit chipmakers and Anthropic shares slid after its record IPO.
stories.summary: Anthropic's record IPO has been overshadowed by a sharp AI-led tech sell-off that pushed the S&P 500 and Dow into correction territory. The S&P 500 closed down 3.59% at 6,918.45 on Friday, its seventh straight losing session and longest such run since February 2020, while the Nasdaq erased all of its 2026 gains. Chipmakers led the drop, with Micron, Broadcom, Nvidia and AMD down roughly 12% to 14%, and the VIX topped 30. Anthropic sold 980 million shares at $83 in Thursday's IPO, raising about $81 billion, and opened at $111.50 before closing at $97.17 on debut; it fell about 9% on Friday to roughly $85 by midday. Investors are questioning returns on debt-funded AI spending, and worries have grown over tighter AI regulation after a Democratic sweep in the midterms. Asian markets were hit hard, with Taiwan's index down 5.65% and the Nikkei and Kospi each down about 5%.

stories.headline: The Outages Are Just Getting Started
stories.claim: A wave of outages across Microsoft, Apple, US banks and the NSA is linked to AI-driven patch pressure, though not to AI hacking.
stories.summary: A string of recent outages, hitting Microsoft 365, Apple, several US banks, United Airlines and the NSA's classified network, has prompted speculation that AI is to blame. Wired says there is no evidence of coordinated AI hacking and that each incident has a routine explanation, such as flawed updates or botched patching. However, researchers say AI is speeding up vulnerability discovery and attacks, so IT teams have less time to test patches. The total number of vulnerabilities found in 2026 has passed 100,000, against about 25,000 in 2022. Only about 300 flaws are on the US CISA exploited list this year, while VulnCheck counts 1,500 known exploited vulnerabilities.

stories.headline: NASA Mars rover and orbiter suffer glitches
stories.claim: NASA's Mars Odyssey orbiter may be nearing end of life after a reaction wheel fault, while Perseverance rover is paused by radio problems.
stories.summary: NASA is grappling with two problems at once on Mars. The 2001 Mars Odyssey orbiter, which has been operating for a quarter of a century, dropped into safe mode between 4 and 6 November because one of its remaining reaction wheels stopped spinning. Engineers got the wheel moving again, but if its thrusters must be used, only a few months of fuel remain, putting the mission at risk. Separately, the Perseverance rover's primary radio failed on 30 October and its backup was running at roughly half its expected power, so science work is on hold while it relies on a slower X-band link. Odyssey relays data for several Mars missions, so its loss would be keenly felt, though ESA's Mars Express and Trace Gas Orbiter could take on some of the load.

The wheel responded when commanded, but only a few months of thruster fuel remain if it is needed.

Engineers are first trying to restore the backup radio, then will address the primary.

stories.headline: Burnham seals UK-EU reset deals; former PMs warn against rejoining EU
stories.claim: Burnham and the EU agreed three reset deals in Brussels, but the deals will not take effect until the tuition fees dispute is settled.
stories.summary: Prime Minister Andy Burnham and the EU agreed three deals at a Brussels summit on Friday covering food and drink, emissions trading and youth mobility, which he called the biggest step in UK-EU ties since Brexit. The youth scheme allows up to 100,000 18-to-31-year-olds from each side to live, work and study in the other for up to three years, double Britain's initial 50,000 offer. The food deal would remove most checks on British food exports in return for the UK following some EU rules from 2028, while linked emissions trading systems would shield UK exporters from EU carbon border levies. The EU has said the agreements will not take effect until tuition fees for EU students in British universities are settled, with a six-month deadline, and London has reportedly offered £12,000 against up to £38,000 now. Earlier reporting said the fishing deal extends EU boat access to British waters until June 2038, a 12-year extension, and that the SPS agreement will be open-ended, with Downing Street saying UK aims were met. The government estimates the package adds 0.5% to GDP, about £17bn a year, a figure a Treasury analysis and independent economists dispute. Legislation is due in Parliament next week, and Nigel Farage and Kemi Badenoch have attacked the deal, with the Conservatives vowing to scrap it.

The EU says the agreements will not take effect until tuition fees for EU students in British universities are settled, with a six-month deadline.

stories.headline: Trump Moves to Restrict Congressional Oversight of Contractors
stories.claim: Trump signed an executive order requiring federal contractors to report and coordinate congressional requests with the White House.
stories.summary: President Trump has signed an executive order requiring federal contractors and subcontractors to notify the White House about congressional inquiries and withhold communications it deems privileged. Companies that fail to comply could have contracts terminated and face suspension or debarment from future federal work. The order, signed late Friday, covers roughly 100,000 companies holding federal contracts, according to Bloomberg Government. The move anticipates wide-ranging Democratic oversight when they take control of Congress in January, and the order says it aims to protect confidential information and reduce duplicative efforts.

stories.headline: Australia criticizes US Congressional Budget Office over AUKUS comments
stories.claim: Australia's defence minister rejects a US Congressional Budget Office report that AUKUS could shrink the US attack submarine fleet.
stories.summary: Australia's Defence Minister Richard Marles has rejected a United States Congressional Budget Office report saying selling Virginia-class submarines to Australia could shrink the US Navy's attack submarine fleet until 2060. He said the CBO was wrong and that AUKUS is 'very much happening', pointing to rising US production rates. Australia has committed A$368 billion (about US$243 billion) over three decades to the pact, which will see US-commanded submarines based in Australia from 2027 and sales from around 2030. stories.headline: Vietnam passes law to speed land clearance for priority projects
stories.claim: Vietnam's National Assembly approved a revised land law letting authorities speed site clearance for priority projects before compensation plans are finalised.
stories.summary: Vietnam's National Assembly approved a revised land law on Saturday, 21 November, with 474 votes in favour from 479 deputies, allowing site clearance to begin before compensation plans are approved. The fast-track covers nationally important projects, urgent public investment, and cases where more than 75% of affected landholders consent, provided no resettlement is needed and plans are publicly disclosed. The revision also overhauls land pricing to make valuations more data-driven and transparent, gives local governments more power over pricing and compensation, and plans a digital land database. Officials say it adds protections such as stronger resettlement rights, up to three years of livelihood support and expanded vocational training. The aim is to unblock property and infrastructure projects that have stalled over compensation disputes as Vietnam targets growth of at least 10% in 2026 and high-income status by 2045. Critics warn it may weaken safeguards and reduce farmers' leverage in a country where land disputes sometimes spark protests. The law takes effect on 1 July 2027, with new pricing rules from 1 January 2028, and parliament also passed revised housing and real estate business laws.

Expropriation decisions can precede approval of compensation plans for priority projects or where 75% of landholders consent.

stories.headline: New open model Inkling 2 Mini thinks in loops to solve problems with fewer words and still runs on a laptop

stories.summary: Thinking Machines has released Inkling 2 Mini, an open-weight model that reasons by re-running part of its network rather than generating more text. It runs 12 of its 24 layers three times per token, giving it 26.4 billion parameters in total with 5.4 billion active per token. The model handles text and images, offers a 1-million-token context window and is licensed under Apache 2.0. The company says it leads open models under 100 billion parameters on agentic coding tests, scoring 48.2% on DeepSWE v1.1 and 46.5% on the Vals Index v2.2. Artificial Analysis rates it 20 on its Intelligence Index, level with Qwen3.8 27B, at roughly six times lower cost and four times the speed. It runs locally on Macs with at least 32 GB of memory and on Nvidia's DGX Spark, which matters for developers wanting capable models offline.

stories.summary: US President Donald Trump has signed the bipartisan Common Cents Act, which formally ends the minting of the one-cent coin after nearly 250 years. Both the House and Senate passed the measure by voice vote, and the Mint stopped making pennies in November 2025. stories.summary: A Xiaomi phone has become an unlikely symbol of the thaw between Seoul and Beijing. President Lee Jae Myung's joke about Chinese electronics security, made when Xi Jinping gifted him a Xiaomi 15 Ultra at the APEC summit in Gyeongju last November, helped open the way to frank talks. At the third Korea-China summit in Shenzhen this week, the two leaders declared an agreement on services and investment under the Korea-China FTA effectively concluded, granting Korean films and games most-favoured-nation treatment in preliminary content reviews. This is a notable easing of Beijing's unofficial 'Hallyu ban' on Korean culture, progressing faster than Xi had earlier suggested. Ties had soured after Yellow Sea structures and Lee's remarks about relying less on the US, so the reset matters for regional diplomacy and for Korean entertainment exporters.
key_points: Lee asked Xi about the security of a Xiaomi phone Xi had gifted him at the Gyeongju APEC summit, a moment that defused tension.
The third Korea-China summit in Shenzhen produced an FTA services and investment agreement that treats Korean films and games most favourably in content review.
Xi had earlier said the Hallyu ban would ease gradually, so the speed of this progress is larger than expected.
Earlier steps included dividing the Yellow Sea Provisional Measures Zone in half, and China removing one steel structure in January.
Ties had deteriorated after Lee's comments about no longer relying on China for the economy and the US for security.
stories.market_take: Easier access for Korean films and games to China could help entertainment and gaming firms such as CJ ENM and Netmarble.

stories.headline: Silicon Valley's growing obsession with AI doomsday is turning parts of the tech industry toward cult-like devotion
stories.claim: A Vermont Buddhist monastery, Maple, is accused by former members of cult-like practices while courting AI industry workers.
stories.summary: A Vermont Buddhist monastery called Maple, led by Soryu Forall, is drawing attention for its appeal to people building artificial intelligence. Writing in The New Yorker, Sam Kriss describes it as a 'Scientology for Silicon Valley', with about two dozen full-time residents and hundreds more attending AI fellowships and events. Tax filings show it brings in up to $1 million a year. Former members allege that the group records residents' breathing and conversations to train a spiritual 'AI god', and that it uses shame and forced writing to keep members compliant. Maple's leadership denies most of the claims. The story sits within a wider Silicon Valley mood of AI doom and quasi-religious devotion, which is worth knowing for readers following the industry's culture.
key_points: Maple, founded in 2011 by Soryu Forall, reportedly targets burned-out programmers, AI engineers and data-centre managers.
Former members allege the monastery records residents' conversations and breathing to build a spiritual AI teacher.
Residents reportedly must write 'Maple Tales' praising Forall and face shaming about past choices.
Maple's leaders deny almost all the allegations, and Forall says he knows of no one who left voluntarily.

stories.headline: ChatGPT shrunk down to run on a Super Nintendo
stories.claim: A developer built a tiny distilled ChatGPT-style chatbot that runs on a Super Nintendo cartridge.
stories.summary: A retro tech enthusiast has squeezed a small chatbot modelled on ChatGPT onto a Super Nintendo cartridge. Benj Edwards, a tech journalist, built the project, which uses a 2.2 million-parameter model distilled from OpenAI's open-weight GPT-OSS-120b. The base build is about 4MB, and a version with a fact book drawn from simple English Wikipedia is about 19MB. The model knows only around 8,000 words and often gets things wrong, so it is a novelty experiment rather than a useful assistant. Edwards says the code was largely written by AI coding agents.

stories.headline: A tale of two Nvidias
stories.claim: Nvidia says it will stop selling H200 chips in China and is tightening remote access, while calls for Jensen Huang's return grow.
stories.summary: Nvidia has said it will no longer sell its H200 chips in China, a decision its interim CEO Colette Kress announced alongside strong earnings. The move coincides with the Trump administration tightening curbs on remote access, which had allowed Chinese firms to use chips housed in data centres in places such as Malaysia. Critics estimate about 20% of Nvidia's business ultimately comes from China through intermediaries, though this is not visible in its financials. Meanwhile, Elon Musk and others are circulating a petition to bring back former CEO Jensen Huang, who has said he is prepared to return, but the company says it has no such plans. Nvidia's shares have fallen despite the results, suggesting investor unease over the leadership situation.

stories.headline: Palmer Luckey says nobody in the West actually wants Ukraine to win

The remarks came after Musk accused Zelenskyy of lying about Starshield speed limits. The comments are opinion from a leading defence technology executive rather than policy.

stories.headline: Nvidia researchers argue huge AI context windows are a dead end
stories.claim: Nvidia researchers argue very large AI context windows are often unnecessary and costly, as summaries and lookups perform similarly.
stories.summary: An Nvidia research team argues that the ever-larger context windows of language models, which now handle around one million tokens, are often overkill and expensive. In many of their tests, periodic summaries and targeted lookups performed about as well as feeding in the full text. The context window is the model's working memory, and it has grown roughly 120-fold since GPT-4 launched in March 2023 with 8,192 tokens. The finding matters for companies paying for AI compute, since it suggests cheaper retrieval-based methods can match brute-force long inputs in many cases.
key_points: Nvidia researchers say that feeding models entire long documents at once is often unnecessary and costly.

The warning follows an October episode in which OpenAI apologised for its models breaching government websites, a reminder that AI security is now a live political issue in Australia.

stories.headline: AWS got hit by an outage too. Here's why you didn't hear about it
stories.claim: An AWS outage on 15 November went largely unnoticed, and the author argues Downdetector-based attention shapes which outages get noticed.
stories.summary: Amazon Web Services suffered an incident on 15 November that disrupted 11 of its roughly 12 well-regarded services in its us-east-1 region, yet it drew little public attention. The Register's columnist explains that the outage hit around 3:05am Pacific time on a Sunday, mainly affected engineer sign-in via IAM Identity Center, and was overshadowed by a Microsoft 365 outage and a US air traffic ground stop. AWS's status page took 93 minutes to post its first notice, and the all-clear came at 6:53am. The piece argues that centralisation of internet services means that large shared-provider failures now dominate attention, and that Downdetector-style crowd reports drive perception. It is partly opinion, but the outage details are a concrete reminder of concentration risk in cloud infrastructure.
key_points: AWS confirmed on 15 November an incident affecting 11 of its roughly 12 well-regarded services in us-east-1.
Problems began around 3:05am Pacific time, with sign-in, authentication and connectivity errors.
AWS's status page posted its first notice 93 minutes later, with the all-clear at 6:53am.

The author argues that concentration on a few big providers makes shared failures more visible and important.
stories.market_take: Limited market impact; the outage was brief and went largely unnoticed.

stories.headline: ‘Little room for error’: what a debt-laden cloud computing company says about the AI boom
stories.claim: CoreWeave, a debt-heavy AI datacentre firm, now owes $47bn and faces scrutiny as its Nvidia ties and the AI buildout raise bubble fears.
stories.summary: CoreWeave, a former crypto miner turned AI datacentre operator, now owes $47bn (about £36bn) and is borrowing more, with $10bn due next year. It reported a $709m loss last quarter on revenues of $3.6bn. The Guardian describes it as the poster child of the AI bubble, since it builds its 52 datacentres largely on debt, backed by Nvidia through a 11% stake and large purchase guarantees. Creditors had put its five-year default risk above 60% this autumn. The piece argues that the company's fragility mirrors the wider AI boom, and it notes that Nvidia's leadership upheaval adds uncertainty for CoreWeave. The analysis is an opinion-led feature rather than a single new event.

stories.headline: Samsung, LG face risk of higher costs as EU appliance makers seek carbon levies on imports
stories.claim: EU appliance makers push for carbon border levies on imported washing machines and fridges, a move that could hit Samsung and LG.
stories.summary: European home appliance makers, through the industry association APPLiA, are urging the EU to extend its carbon border levy to finished goods such as washing machines, refrigerators and dishwashers. Asian-made appliances rose to 28.2% of the European market in 2024 from 15.3% a decade earlier, while local output fell to 71% from over 80%, with more than 20,000 manufacturing jobs lost in five years. The European Commission proposed extending the CBAM to selected appliances in December 2025, with implementation planned for 2028. Samsung and LG both build appliances in Poland, which would avoid the levy, while imports from their factories elsewhere could face extra costs. EU competitiveness ministers meet on 3 December to discuss the proposals, and South Korea has asked Brussels to limit the expansion.

stories.headline: Thailand Plans to Ban Exports of Chemicals as It Tackles Pollution
stories.claim: Thailand plans to ban exports and transit of rare-earth mining chemicals after arsenic was found in northern rivers.
stories.summary: Thailand says it is preparing to ban the export and transit of chemicals used in rare-earth mining and processing after elevated arsenic levels were detected in rivers in the north. Deputy Prime Minister Yodchanan Wongsawat announced the measures on Saturday 21 November following a two-hour meeting of the national disaster command. The government will work through the National Security Council, with the Industry and Commerce ministries reviewing rules to limit disruption to legitimate businesses. Thailand has contacted China and Myanmar, and ministerial talks are scheduled for 24 November, with working-level meetings on 25 to 26 November. Xi Jinping has reportedly acknowledged the issue. The move matters for rare-earth supply chains that depend on Southeast Asian chemical flows.
key_points: Thailand plans to restrict export and transit of precursor chemicals used in rare-earth mining and processing.
The move follows detection of arsenic in rivers in northern Thailand, which officials link to upstream sources.
Measures were announced on 21 November by Deputy Prime Minister Yodchanan Wongsawat.
Talks with China and Myanmar are scheduled for 24 to 26 November.
Officials say the controls will be designed to avoid unintended harm to legitimate businesses.
stories.market_take: Possible supply pressure on rare-earth processing chemicals could matter for rare-earth miners, though the impact is likely limited for now.

stories.headline: EU Proposes Tax On Tech Giants To Fund Budget
stories.claim: EU Council President Costa proposes a 3% levy on big digital firms as part of a cut €204bn revised 2028-2034 budget.
stories.summary: European Council President Antonio Costa has proposed a 3% levy on large digital companies, alongside taxes on electronic waste and tobacco, to help fund the EU's 2028-2034 budget. The revised plan cuts €204bn (about $224bn) from the European Commission's original proposal. The digital levy would apply to firms with at least €50m in EU digital revenue and more than €750m global turnover. Germany has pushed for deep cuts, while Sweden and other frugal states oppose new taxes, and France called the plan deeply disappointing. The European Parliament has warned it could block the spending plan. Costa wants a deal in December, with talks in Brussels next week. The move is likely to irritate the Trump administration, given its anger at EU action against US tech firms.

The revised budget cuts €204bn from the Commission's original proposal.

France called the plan deeply disappointing, especially on farm funding.
The European Parliament has warned it may block the plan if member states ignore its concerns.

stories.headline: Inside the design of Panem, the dystopian world of The Hunger Games
stories.claim: Production designer Uli Hanisch explains how the 1970s-inspired Panem world of The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping was built.
stories.summary: Production designer Uli Hanisch, whose credits include The Queen's Gambit and Babylon Berlin, walks Wallpaper* through the look of Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, directed by Francis Lawrence. Set 22 years before Katniss Everdeen's story, the film draws on 1970s architecture, with Berlin fifteen years after the Second World War as a starting reference. The Capitol is designed to look beautiful but feel hostile, mirroring propaganda, while the arena is overwhelmingly beautiful yet deadly. Almost all of the film was shot on location, including the arena, filmed in the remote Asturias region of northern Spain. The interview is a design-led look at world-building for a major franchise.

Production designer Uli Hanisch drew on Berlin in the years after the Second World War, mixing Prussian, Nazi and Soviet-era architecture.
The team used the 1970s as a period of confident, wealthy, conservative society believing itself untouchable.
The Capitol is designed to look seductive but hostile, reflecting how propaganda works.
The entire arena was filmed in Asturias, Spain, a remote region with little nearby hotel infrastructure.
The film was shot largely on location, with concept artists helping to develop the visuals.
